rationale: The depreciation-surprise leg is byte-identical to the archive's strongest signal (Depreciation Conservatism Book Interaction) and only the value leg is swapped from book/market to book-EV/EV — a third cosmetic variant of the same family after the book and asset-yield versions, with no diagnosis of why the leverage/cash adjustment should matter.

This is essentially the sign-mirrored, unscaled twin of the archived "Underdepreciation Earnings Reliance Trap" (same earnings-yield rank leg, same dp/at vs MA(dp/at,3) surprise), and the hypothesis wording is muddled since the value leg uses reported ib, which is mechanically depressed by the very depreciation elevation being rewarded.

Netting the depreciation-surprise leg against asset-scaled working-capital accruals is a genuinely new composite that tests whether the accrual channel adds incrementally to the archive's best depreciation result, though there is a real risk the known-strong depreciation leg simply dominates a noisy accrual term that has repeatedly failed in this archive.

Internally inconsistent mechanism — operating cash flow adds depreciation back and is essentially invariant to depreciation policy, so "cheap cash flow supported by understated asset consumption" does not follow; it is also just the archived Underdepreciation Earnings Reliance Trap with oancf substituted for ib in the value leg.

Another value-leg swap onto the already-tested depreciation-conservatism interaction, with a weaker link (dividends are a cash payout only loosely tied to depreciation policy) and likely reduced, dividend-payer-only coverage that risks overstating improvement.

TREND(dp/at,3) is nearly the same information as the archived asset-yield signal's dp/at minus MA(dp/at,3) deviation, making this a smoothing-level cosmetic variant of a signal already evaluated (and the related MA3−MA5 persistence variant already failed).
